c.tagline: Iraq's holiest pilgrimage city, where two golden shrines face each other.

taxi.fareNote: Meters are rarely used; agree the fare with the driver before setting off, or share a per-seat 'service' taxi on fixed routes. App-based ride-hailing coverage is thin, and during Arba'een most pilgrims cross the shrine district on foot.

emergency.note: National emergency line 112; fire 115. Ambulance service can be limited, so private hospitals or your embassy's line may be faster. Security is heavy around the shrines.

avoid.reason: Stay within the well-secured shrine city and main routes; avoid rural desert areas toward the Anbar border due to residual security risks.
Around the Imam Hussein and Abbas shrines, dense pilgrimage crowds bring pickpocketing and crush risk, and expect frequent security checkpoints requiring your passport.

hood_desc: The pedestrianised plaza and surrounding lanes linking the Imam Husayn and Al-Abbas shrines, lined with hotels, tea houses, bookshops and souvenir stalls; the prime, walk-everywhere base for pilgrims.

The dense historic core wrapped around the Imam Husayn Shrine, with the covered bazaar, religious schools and the highest concentration of guesthouses; convenient but very crowded during Muharram and Arba'een.
A newer, more spread-out residential quarter east of the shrines with modern hotels and lower rates; quieter and a short taxi ride from the holy sites.
The area around the historic Baghdad Gate on the northern edge of the old town, full of markets, cheap eateries and transport links, within walking distance of the shrines.
A calmer suburban district southwest toward Najaf, built around the domed shrine of Hurr ibn Yazid al-Riyahi; residential and green, popular for a quieter stay away from the crowds.

transit.pay: Fares are paid in cash directly to the driver; there is no rechargeable transit card. Shared 'service' taxis on fixed routes are far more common than public buses and are paid per seat in dinars.
transit.hours: Buses and shared taxis run roughly 6am-10pm; after that, private taxis fill the gap.
transit.note: Public transit is minimal; most pilgrims and residents rely on shared service taxis, private cars and walking. Foot traffic around the shrines is enormous, and during Arba'een the whole shrine district becomes a pedestrian zone.

train: Iraqi Republic Railways runs limited pilgrimage-season services linking Baghdad and Karbala
bus: Intercity buses and shared 'service' taxis to Najaf (~80 km), Baghdad (~100 km) and Hillah from the city's garages

transit.m: Shared 'service' taxi or pilgrim coach to Karbala (~1.5 hr)

tip.r: Not expected; rounding up a taxi or restaurant bill is appreciated. Much service around the shrines is driven by hospitality to pilgrims rather than tipping.
